sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.

(a) Real SO-101 and its digital twin. (b) The four tasks. (c) Sim2real: five policies trained without real data keep their ranking on the real robot. (d) Leaderboard. (e) Harness ablation. (f) The language model matters. policy reaches 95.1% on LIBERO [16], where clean averages for three protocol-faithful vision-languageaction model (VLA) and world-action model (WAM) evaluations span only 1.36 points [17]. Real2sim evaluation [18, 19, 20, 21] shows that carefully built digital twin can predict real-world rankings, but the prediction is specific to the simulator, policies and setup on which it was validated: in five-policy study spanning 1,115 real rollouts across three simulators, SIMPLER showed weak ranking agreement with the real robot [22]. These studies also mostly run in one direction, placing policies trained on real data inside twin. As policies are increasingly trained on simulated data alone [23, 24], benchmark should also show that its ranking survives when the same sim-trained weights run on real robot. Finally, it should measure what aggregate success hides: policy can complete task without understanding it: on LIBERO, probe that replaces instruction text with task-ID embedding nearly matches the best published results [25], and on real SO-101, VLAs that manipulate reliably can fail to adapt to OOD spatial relations [10]. We introduce SO-101 Bench, simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation with single SO-101 arm, built so that its rankings carry over to the real robot  (Fig. 1)  . Its core is an Isaac Lab [26] digital twin of real SO-101 setup with 138 household objects in three generalization splits: seen (in the training dataset), unseen object of seen class, and unseen class, with 37 unseen-class objects kept private. Four tasks (place every object in bin; place an object next to another; place it between two others; move it in direction until it reaches the boundary object) are scored automatically from simulator state. They require the policy to pick out the named object among same-class distractors, grasp unfamiliar geometry and place it under spatial constraints. The primary evaluation has 916 feasibility-checked episodes over 15 task-family split cells, with subsets for held-out appearances (ROBUST), rotating an object to fit tight space (PLAN) and remembering occluded objects (MEM). Every learned policy is fine-tuned on the same 3,629 simulated teleoperated demonstrations of seen objects under an equal 36 4 A100 compute budget. Two studies test whether the twin can stand in for the real robot. Independently trained real-only and sim-only GR00T N1.6 policies find the same conditions hard (Pearson = 0.86 across the 15 cells) and fail in the same ways (Sec. 4). Five policies that never saw real data from our setup, four VLAs and an LLM agent, then run with identical weights in the twin and on the physical SO-101 in an environment unseen in training, with objects from all three splits; SO-101 Bench policies work out of the box in unseen real environments with unseen objects. Simulation ranks them exactly as the real robot does (Spearman ρ = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000, 95% CI [0.000, 0.169]), although it overestimates every policys success by 9 to 31 percentage points (Sec. 5). On the full leaderboard of nine VLAs and WAMs, the best learned policies, InternW0- [27] and Galaxea 0.5 [28], are statistically tied near 61; spatial placement and unseen classes are where they fail, and none exceeds 17% on PLAN. The strongest entry is an LLM agent: GPT-6.1 Sol [29] writing code in the PyRUA-Lean harness [30] and handing grasps to Galaxea 0.5 scores 83.2 and solves 75% of PLAN. Its lead comes largely from the harness. On 60 paired episodes, Sol succeeds on 35% (21/60) with direct tool calls, 67% (40/60) with PyRUA-Lean and 85% (51/60) with the Galaxea 0.5 hand-off, against 53% (32/60) for Galaxea 0.5 alone, and the lead holds on the real robot, 64% (29/45) against 53% (24/45). Our contributions are: SO-101 Bench, digital-twin benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation on low-cost arm, with instanceand class-level object splits, ROBUST, PLAN and MEM subsets and automatic scoring, released with the so101_bench_sim (3,629 simulated episodes) and so101_bench_real (4,400 real episodes) datasets. Evidence that the twin ranks policies as the real robot does: conditionand failure-level correspondence between independently trained real-only and sim-only policies, and an exact sim2real ranking of five policies, including an LLM agent, run with identical weights and no real data from our setup; these policies perform language-conditioned tasks out of the box in an unseen real environment with unseen objects. leaderboard of nine VLAs and WAMs and two LLM agents, with every learned policy fine-tuned on the same data and compute, showing that spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remain open. Harness and model ablations showing that, in our setting, code-as-policy harness that hands grasping to learned policy outperforms either on their own; Direct action generation by the agent proves expensive and ineffective, and 6.1 Sol compares favorably to other agents.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Low-cost hardware and SO-101 benchmarks. Cheap hardware has repeatedly widened who can do robot learning. ALOHA showed that low-cost bimanual rig can learn fine manipulation [31], and 2026 platforms push prices further, from $1,688 bimanual mobile manipulator [32] to the SO-101, at about fortieth of the price of an ALOHA arm [4]. LeRobot [5] and community data have made the SO-100/101 training platform for open VLAs [6, 7]. Four 2026 benchmarks evaluate VLAs on physical SO-101 arms. Yu and Qiu [8] analyse failure and recovery on four tasks, VLA-REPLICA is sub-$1,100 kit reproduced across sites [9], ArmnetBench scores 2,518 rollouts of seven policies on an arm farm [3], and Spa-Bench probes recombinations of familiar objects, spatial concepts and actions in its primary evaluation, with separate novel-object pilot [10]. All four use real robot demonstrations for task-specific adaptation and evaluate on physical hardware. In simulation, the SO-101 Task Set contains eight language-free tasks for visual reinforcement learning with sim2real transfer [15], and LeIsaac provides SO-101 teleoperation and data-collection tooling in Isaac Lab [33]. To our knowledge, SO-101 Bench is the first language-conditioned SO-101 benchmark with held-out object splits whose simulated policy ranking is validated on the real arm. It also represents one of, if not the most, challenging task suites handled by an SO-101 up to this point. Real2sim evaluation and sim2real transfer. Whether simulated evaluation predicts real performance was studied early for navigation [34]; for manipulation, SIMPLER [18] showed that an aligned simulator can rank 3 real-world policies and introduced the MMRV metric. Twins built from scans, neural reconstructions or generated assets now report strong score or ranking agreement within their validated settings [19, 20, 35, 36, 37, 38]; SimFoundry reaches Pearson 0.911 and MMRV 0.018 over five policy architectures [21]. Two 2026 results temper this. Validity does not carry across setups: re-tested against new real rollouts, SIMPLERs agreement with the real-robot ranking is weak [22]. Reconstruction quality also matters: an authored object-and-scene pipeline achieved simreal correlation of 0.90 versus 0.51 for default reconstruction in ten-cell study [39], consistent with our tuning of each reconstructed object against its physical counterpart (Appendix E). Learned world models are an alternative evaluator [40], but released models often predict success on verified failures [41]. In parallel, policies trained only on simulated data now transfer to real robots: MolmoB0T reaches 79.2% on real pick-andplace without real demonstrations [23], OASIS pairs image-to-3D assets with teleoperation inside simulation [24], and LEGS and Splat2Act fine-tune pretrained VLAs using only synthetic robot demonstrations [42, 43]. We deploy five sim-trained policies, including an LLM agent, with identical weights and test whether their ranking survives. LLM agents for manipulation. Language models have long planned over learned skills [44] or written programs that compose perception and control [45, 46], and hierarchical systems pair high-level language reasoning with low-level action generation [47, 48]. In 2026 such agents became competitive with end-toend policies: coding agents are now benchmarked on manipulation directly [49, 50, 51]; GPT-6 Astra with direct end-effector tool calls ranked above all forty public-policy entries in its September 2026 RoboDojo comparison [52, 53]; RoboICL reports higher aggregate progress than its strongest listed baseline on thirty-task subset [54], and PyRUA-Lean exceeds the best public entries in its reported leaderboard snapshot [30]. parallel line treats the VLA as tool: Harness VLA exposes frozen VLA as retryable contact-rich primitive [55], VoLo steers one as an interruptible tool [56], Gemini Robotics ER 2 hands motor execution to any VLA [57], and systematic study of such hierarchies finds that model choice and interface jointly shape performance [58]. Harness effects are large. With the same planner and primitives, one study reports that writing code instead of calling tools raises success from 63.1% to 71.7% [30]; better harness lets weaker model beat stronger one [59]; and outside robotics the scaffold alone moves accuracy by up to 28 points within one model [60]. These studies usually compare agents with published entries trained under each entrys own protocol. Simulated agent evaluations, ours included, commonly pause the simulator while the model computes, which hides its real-time cost [61], and frontier models controlling physical arms directly are not yet precise or efficient enough to finish tasks within practical action budget [62]. SO-101 Bench compares agents and learned policies on the same episodes after training every learned policy on the same data and compute, ablates harness and model separately, and runs the agent on the real robot. Manipulation benchmarks and evaluation practice. Simulated benchmarks for generalist policies [12, 13, 14, 53, 63] face saturation and traintest overlap. LIBERO instruction conditioning largely selects among memorized tasks [16]; policies above 90% there fall below 30%, or to zero, under modest perturbations [64, 65]; and an audit of five suites finds shortcut solvability, state-of-the-art gains not established as statistically significant, creeping overfitting and dependence on the training-data source [25]. Responses include generalization suites [66, 63], capability suites for memory of occluded objects [67] and spatial grounding [10]. Real-world evaluation has moved to distributed pairwise comparison [68], autonomous evaluation cells [69], and statistical methods that separate policies with few trials [11, 70]. SO-101 Bench adopts several of these lessons: it separates unseen instances from unseen classes and keeps part of the latter private, fine-tunes every policy on the same seen-object data under one compute budget, selects checkpoints on separate validation set, and reports confidence intervals over 916 episodes. It also scores two spatial skills that, to our knowledge, few benchmarks test in closed loop: placing an object between two referents, and rotating grasped object to fit (PLAN). 4 Figure 2: The four SO-101 Bench tasks. Bin, next-to, between and directional move, with the target paths overlaid on successful simulation episodes. The task panels repeat Fig. 1b.

sections.title: 3 SO-101 Bench
sections.content: SO-101 Bench evaluates language-conditioned tabletop manipulation with single SO-101 arm [1]. It is designed to test whether policy can turn semantic understanding into precise physical execution: identifying the right object among distractors, grasping objects of unfamiliar geometry, and placing them under (often precise) spatial constraints. Every component below is shared by all evaluated policies.

sections.title: 3.1 Tasks
sections.content: The benchmark comprises four language-conditioned tasks  (Fig. 2)  , scored as five task families. Place each object in the plastic bin. The pure grasping task: the policy must identify, grasp, transport and deposit every object on the table. The bin moves between episodes. We evaluate 1-object and 4-object condition as separate families. Place [object 1] next to [object 2]. The policy must place the target close to referent without disturbing other objects, adding semantic grounding and basic spatial placement. Place [object 1] between [object 2] and [object 3]. The target must end centred between two referents, which makes the task sensitive to object extent, orientation and fine placement; it is the most demanding task. Move [object 1] [direction]. The policy must push or carry the target along straight path in commanded direction until it reaches the boundary formed by the next object in its way. The bin task stresses grounding, grasp strategy and grasp precision; the three spatial tasks additionally require relational grounding, spatial reasoning, fine-grained placement and robustness to partial occlusion. To keep language grounding nontrivial, distractors of the same class or colour are included so that class identity alone is insufficient, and colour words are omitted from instructions unless necessary (i.e when two objects of the same class are on the table). 5 Figure 3: Simulation objects by generalization split. Orange dots mark physical objects that are also used in the real-robot evaluation. The 37 private unseen-class objects are held out to prevent test-set leakage and are not shown.

sections.title: 3.2 Objects and Generalization Splits
sections.content: The benchmark uses 138 household objects in three generalization splits  (Fig. 3)  : seen (48 objects that appear in training), unseen object, seen class (43 objects whose class, e.g. bowl or pen, appears in training but whose instance does not), and unseen class (47 objects of entirely novel classes). The splits separate transfer across instances from transfer across categories. Objects were chosen to maximize diversity of geometry and of domain (e.g. office, kitchen, sports, toys), with priority on irregular shapes. Every object was verified through teleoperation to be graspable by the SO-101, so that failures reflect the policy rather than the hardware. Of the unseen-class objects, 37 are kept private to prevent test-set leakage. All objects were created using the image-to-3D tools in 3D AI Studio [71]. The 60 physical objects were reconstructed from photographs of the real items and their simulated appearance and physical properties were tuned to match them; the remaining objects were generated from internet or AI-generated images and passed through the same pipeline (Appendix E). All simulated objects are rigid bodies.

sections.title: 3.3 Digital Twin
sections.content: All evaluation runs in digital twin of the original real-world setup, built in Isaac Lab [26] from scan of the room and the object assets of Sec. 3.2. Physics runs at 240 Hz and the policy acts at 30 Hz. Policies observe an overhead camera and wrist camera, both at 640 480, and the arms joint positions. The twin includes 22 background environments: 18 are used in training and in the varied evaluation episodes, and 4 are held out (Appendix F). The robot is rendered in one of 6 training colours or one of 4 held-out colours. The real arms joint calibration is aligned to the simulated kinematics so that the same policy weights can run in both domains (Sec. 5).

sections.title: 3.4 Scoring
sections.content: Episodes are scored automatically from simulator state. Positions are measured in the tabletop plane from where objects rest at the start of the episode. success condition must hold continuously for 5 s; failure condition ends the episode once it has held for 5 s, so briefly undoing mistake is allowed. The robot is considered to touch an object when any link presses on it with more than 0.05 N. Episodes time out after 30 (75 for 4-object bins). Bin: every object ends with its reference point (the centre of its top-down bounding box) inside the bins footprint and untouched by the robot. Fails if the bin moves more than 0.5 in. 6 Figure 4: PLAN and MEM examples (start, middle and end of successful primary-evaluation episodes). Left: GPT-6.1 Sol with PyRUA-Lean and Galaxea 0.5 rotates the toy boat to fit between the pill planner and the camera (episode 529), which all nine learned policies fail. Right: ImageWAM moves the tape backwards (episode 300), retaining the boundary object position while it is occluded during the move; four of the nine learned policies solve this episode. All objects and backgrounds shown are public. Next to: the targets top-down outline ends within 2 in of the referents outline. Between: the targets reference point ends within 1.75 in of the line through the two referents reference points, and closer to each referent than the referents are to each other. Move: with an object ahead of the target, the targets leading edge ends within 2 in of that objects facing edge; otherwise the target advances at least 2 in. The target must stay within 2 in of the straight path, and the boundary object must not move more than 0.5 in along the direction. In all three spatial tasks the target must move at least 1 in and must not be touched by the robot at the end, and the episode fails if any non-target object (referents included) moves more than 1 in, or if the target or held object stays in contact with another object for more than 5 s.

sections.title: 3.5 Training Data
sections.content: All learned policies are fine-tuned on so101_bench_sim: 3,629 teleoperated episodes (18.5 at 30 fps) recorded in the digital twin using seen objects only. It contains 1,892 bin episodes (including bin instructions that name single target among other objects), 1,150 next-to and between episodes, and 587 move episodes; 3,004 episodes have four objects on the table. Most episodes are rendered with randomized lighting, camera intrinsics and extrinsics, background and robot colour; the canonical setup remains in the training distribution. variant, so101_bench_sim_WM, adds the episodes initial overhead and wrist frames for policies that accept them. We also release so101_bench_real, approximately 4,400 real-robot teleoperated episodes (20 h) across approximately 35 objects.

sections.title: 3.6 Primary Evaluation
sections.content: The primary evaluation contains 916 scored episodes spanning the 15 task-family split cells, with every object appearing in each family it supports. Feasibility (spacing between objects) is checked for every layout so that poor arrangement cannot make success impossible. About half the episodes use the canonical appearance and half vary the background and robot colour. We report the benchmark score, the mean success rate over the 15 cells, with 95% bootstrap confidence interval that resamples episodes within cells. Three overlapping subsets probe specific capabilities: ROBUST (178 episodes with held-out backgrounds and robot colours), PLAN (48 episodes in which the grasped object must be rotated to fit into tight space), and MEM (51 episodes in which the policy must remember the position and 3D footprint of an object that becomes occluded). Figure 4 shows successful example of each.

sections.title: 3.7 Fine-Tuning Protocol
sections.content: Every learned policy is fine-tuned with an equal compute budget of 36 on 4A100-80GB GPUs, following its authors recommended recipe where one exists (Appendix C). Checkpoints are evaluated on heldout 39-episode validation set, and the best checkpoint is used for the primary evaluation. sections.title: 4 Real-Only vs. Sim-Only Policy Correspondence
sections.content: Before measuring sim2real transfer (Sec. 5), we ask coarser question: does the digital twin reproduce the difficulty structure of the real benchmark? If policy trained in simulation and evaluated in the twin finds the same tasks, splits and failure modes hard as policy trained and evaluated in the real world, the twin is useful proxy for real-world evaluation even before any weights cross domains. Setup. We fine-tune two GR00T N1.6-3B policies [72, 74] independently: real-only policy on real teleoperated demonstrations (so101_bench_real), evaluated on the physical SO-101, and sim-only policy on demonstrations collected in the digital twin (a subset of so101_bench_sim containing 3D scanned objects from so101_bench_real, with 50% of the data volume of so101_bench_real), evaluated in simulation. We compare them on 906 episodes matched across domains by task, instruction, ordered object set and object split. Object poses are not identical across domains, so individual episodes are not exact replicas; the primary comparison is therefore at the level of the 15 task split conditions and of failure composition, with episode-level agreement reported as secondary measure. Real-world outcomes and failure types were labelled by hand; simulated failures were labelled the same way and both were mapped to three categories, semantic (wrong object or referent(s)), grasping (grasp, lift or release failed) and placement (correct object handled, imprecise/incorrect placement). Difficulty is preserved across conditions. The sim-only policy succeeds on 45% (409/906) of episodes and the real-only policy on 61% (552/906), gap of 15.8 pp (95% CI [19.9, 11.8]). Despite this offset, the two systems order the 15 conditions similarly: Pearson = 0.86 [0.71, 0.91] and Spearman ρ = 0.74 [0.52, 0.91] across cells (Fig. 5a). In both domains success is highest on the 1-object bin and seen objects and falls with task difficulty and object novelty, with the 4-object bin and the between task hardest on unseen classes. Failure modes are preserved. The composition of failures on the spatial tasks follows the same trend in both domains (Fig. 5b). On seen objects most failures are placement errors (69% real, 62% sim; total variation distance 0.07); on unseen classes most are semantic or grasping errors (74% real, 93% sim). Across all splits the two failure mixes differ by total variation distance of 0.13. On the 4-object bin, the real-only policy bins 67% of objects and the sim-only policy 47%; per-episode progress is weakly correlated across domains, likely due to the small size of the sim dataset for this experiments (Spearman ρ = 0.35; Fig. 5c). Episode-level agreement is moderate. Paired episodes have the same outcome 66% of the time (MCC 0.36), and where both failed the failure type matches in 47% of cases (Cohens κ = 0.17). This is expected given differeing training dataset scales, initial poses and stochastic policies, and is why we emphasize condition-level correspondence. Full results are in Appendix A. Overall, because the two policies differ in training data as well as in evaluation domain, this experiment cannot attribute the absolute gap to the simulator; the lower sim success reflects both policies and domains together. What it does show is that the twin reproduces which conditions are hard and why policies fail there. Section 5 isolates the simulator by running identical weights (with sim training only) in both domains.

sections.title: 5 Sim2Real with No Real Data
sections.content: A simulated benchmark is only useful if it tells us which policies are better in the real world. We test this directly: five policies that never saw real data from our setup are evaluated, with identical weights, both in the digital twin and on the physical SO-101. Setup. We evaluate four learned policies, Galaxea 0.5 [28], GR00T N1.7 [73], π0.5 [48] and MolmoAct2SO101 [7], and the strongest LLM agent, GPT-6.1 Sol (PyRUA) + Galaxea 0.5, with the same checkpoints and harness as the leaderboard (Sec. 6). The learned policies were fine-tuned only on simulated demonstrations; the agent pairs frozen language model with the same sim-trained Galaxea 0.5 checkpoint, to which it hands 9 Figure 6: Sim2real. (a) Policy-level success on the real robot (unseen environment) vs. simulation (many environments) on the same 45 layouts: the ranking of all five policies is preserved exactly (Spearman ρ = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000) and every policy scores higher in simulation. Diamond: the LLM agent; circles: learned policies fine-tuned only on simulated demonstrations. (b) Success in simulation and on the real robot per policy, overall (45 episodes) and per task family (9 episodes), with 95% Wilson intervals. Bottom: the agent on matched trial 41, between episode with unseen-class objects that none of the four learned policies solved on the real robot. Galaxea 0.5 grasps the tongs, then the agent carries and places them, in both domains. off grasping. The evaluation set has 45 episodes: 3 for each of the 15 task-family split cells, using only the 40 benchmark objects we still own physically (18 seen, 11 unseen object, 11 unseen class), with every object used at least once. Each layout is reproduced on the real table by projecting the simulated object footprints into the overhead camera view, so both domains start from matched object positions and poses. The real robot operates in an environment that does not appear in the training data, and real episodes are scored by the operator under the benchmarks success and failure rules and the same time limits. As in simulation, the agents time limit counts control steps only: the arm holds still while the model computes. Median elapsed wall time to rollout stop is 197 for the agent, compared with 38 for Galaxea 0.5, 38 for GR00T N1.7, 59 for π0.5 and 56 for MolmoAct2-SO101 over the same 45 layouts, including successes and failures. These times come from timestamped control traces checked against the original recordings and include inference waits and within-rollout stalls, but exclude model/server startup, scene resets and subsequent operator scoring (Appendix B). Lighting and camera placement are fixed for the whole study. The four learned policies are evaluated in alternating blocks so that slow drift does not favour any one of them, and the agent in later session in the same environment; before every episode the overhead view is compared with reference frame (across all 225 real episodes the camera moved by at most 2.6 px and brightness changed by at most 7%). In simulation each layout is run once with the canonical appearance. Simulation preserves the policy ranking. Success in simulation and on the real robot ranks the five policies identically (Fig. 6a): GPT-6.1 Sol (PyRUA) + Galaxea 0.5 84% (38/45) vs. 64% (29/45), Galaxea 0.5 67% (30/45) vs. 53% (24/45), GR00T N1.7 56% (25/45) vs. 24% (11/45), π0.5 49% (22/45) vs. 18% (8/45), and MolmoAct2-SO101 24% (11/45) vs. 16% (7/45). The Spearman correlation is 1.00 and the mean maximum rank violation (MMRV [18]) is 0.000 (95% CI [0.000, 0.169], resampling episodes within each policy); the Pearson correlation is 0.90 [0.66, 0.97]. The ranking spans two kinds of system, an LLM agent that plans and places through code and four end-to-end policies, so it does not depend on the policies sharing an architecture. With five policies these intervals remain wide, and we treat the result as evidence that simulation ranks policies correctly rather than as precise calibration. The agents lead transfers. On the real robot the agent succeeds on 29 of 45 episodes against 24 for Galaxea 0.5, the policy it calls for grasping: it solves 10 episodes that Galaxea 0.5 fails and fails 5 that Galaxea 0.5 solves (exact McNemar = 0.30; in simulation 10 against 2, = 0.04). Its advantage lies where it, rather than Galaxea 0.5, does the work. It succeeds on 8 of 9 real next-to episodes, against 2 for Galaxea 0.5, and on 7 of 15 unseen-class episodes, against 4. Eight real episodes were solved by the agent and by none of the four learned policies, including the between episode with unseen-class objects in Fig. 6 (bottom). None of the agents 16 real failures involved the wrong object: 7 were on the bin tasks (5 knocked the lighter real bin), 3 moved non-target object, and the remaining 6 missed the placement criteria (for example, by setting the target on top of referent). Simulation is optimistic, by different amounts per policy. Every policy succeeds more often in simulation, by 9 to 31 percentage points (20 for the agent). Paired episodes agree on the outcome 5691% of the time, and almost all disagreements are episodes that succeed in simulation and fail on the real robot (57, against 10 the other way). The gap is largest on the bin tasks for GR00T N1.7 and on the bin and move tasks for π0.5 (Fig. 6b): for example, GR00T bins the single object in 9/9 simulated episodes but 3/9 real ones; each policys low real-world success rate on bin tasks is, however, largely explained by the far lesser mass of the real plastic bin (making it easier to displace). Many larger real objects were also scaled down to 0.70.9 times their real-world size in simulation. Overall, absolute success rates in simulation should be read as an upper bound on real-world performance, while comparisons between policies transfer. Per-family and per-split results are in Appendix B.

sections.title: 6 Leaderboard
sections.content: We evaluate nine learned policies and two LLM agents on the full primary evaluation  (Fig. 7)  . Policies. The learned policies cover two families. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) map images and language directly to actions: GR00T N1.7 [73], π0.5 [48], Galaxea 0.5 [28], and MolmoAct2 [7], which we fine-tune from two starting points, the general MolmoAct2 checkpoint (base) and its SO-100/101 post-trained variant (SO101). World-action models (WAMs) additionally model future observations: InternW0- [27] and FLUX 3 Action [75] jointly model video and actions, ImageWAM [76] uses an image-editing backbone, and 11 Figure 7: SO-101 Bench leaderboard (916 primary-evaluation episodes). Score is the mean success over the 15 task object-split cells with 95% bootstrap CI; tiles give raw success by object split, task and evaluation subset (ROBUST: held-out backgrounds and robot colours; PLAN: rotate to fit; MEM: remember occluded objects). Bold marks the best learned policy in each column. Diamonds: LLM agents; circles: VLAs; squares: WAMs. LaWAM [77] predicts DINOv3 [78] latent states. All learned policies are fine-tuned on so101_bench_sim under the protocol of Sec. 3.7; FLUX 3 Action is fine-tuned with LoRA [79], following its released recipe, and the rest are fine-tuned in full or with their recommended frozen components (Appendix C). The two LLM agents pair frozen language model (GPT-6.1 Sol [29] or DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 [80]) with code-as-policy harness [45], PyRUA-Lean [30], that hands grasping to Galaxea 0.5; we analyse them in Sec. 7. Learned policies fall short of the benchmark. The best learned policies, InternW0- (61.4, 95% CI [58.5, 64.1]) and Galaxea 0.5 (60.8 [57.9, 63.6]), are statistically tied, followed by GR00T N1.7 (45.8), ImageWAM (43.0), π0.5 (41.0) and LaWAM (39.9). Both MolmoAct2 variants score below 25 and FLUX 3 Action scores 8.0. Starting MolmoAct2 from its SO-100/101 checkpoint does not help (20.9 vs. 23.8 for the base model, with overlapping intervals), so prior exposure to the embodiment (in its current form) is no substitute for the benchmarks task and object coverage under this protocol. Training scale appears to drive performance. Under the equal 36 hr budget, the number of fine-tuning samples each policy sees varies by factor of 30 (Appendix C), and the amount of robot data in its pretraining varies widely as well. The strongest learned policies combine large robot pretraining corpora with at least full epoch of fine-tuning (InternW01.2 epochs, Galaxea 0.5 1.6), whereas the three weakest saw well under one epoch: MolmoAct2 0.50.6 epochs and FLUX 3 Action 0.2; both appear under-trained. The MolmoAct2 training loss was still falling steeply when the budget ran out, and its published simulation recipe uses about five times as many samples [7]; FLUX 3 Actions LoRA run used less than tenth of the samples in its released full fine-tuning recipe [75]. These results therefore rank policies at fixed compute budget, and the low scores of MolmoAct2 and FLUX 3 Action should not be read as their capability ceiling. Spatial tasks and novel objects are the bottleneck. Grasping familiar objects is largely solved: the strongest learned policies bin single object in 9093% of episodes and place 90% of objects in 4-object bins. The spatial tasks are far harder, with next-to and between success of 3444% for the same policies. Object novelty compounds this. On the spatial tasks, InternW0falls from 72% on seen objects to 18% on unseen classes for next to, and from 56% to 19% for between; Galaxea 0.5 falls from 71% to 19% and from 63% to 12%. Pooled 12 Figure 8: Episodes solved only by GPT-6.1 Sol + PyRUA-Lean v9.6 + Galaxea 0.5. Initial overhead views, cropped to the task workspace, with the exact instructions. All ten other leaderboard entries failed each episode. Episodes 174 and 471 belong to PLAN. over tasks, the six strongest learned policies lose 3043 points between seen objects and unseen classes; the three weakest lose less only because their seen-object success is already low. Subsets isolate distinct weaknesses. PLAN is the clearest gap: no learned policy exceeds 17% when the grasped object must be rotated to fit (GR00T N1.7 is best), while the agent reaches 75%. On MEM, learned policies reach at most 47% (InternW0-, which has native memory [27]). ROBUST separates policies by visual robustness rather than skill: Galaxea 0.5 and GR00T N1.7 keep their overall success under held-out backgrounds and robot colours, whereas LaWAM drops from 39% to 18% and ImageWAM from 43% to 34%. LLM agents lead. Both agents outperform every learned policy, including the Galaxea 0.5 policy they call: GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 83.2 [80.7, 85.7] and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 66.8 [63.7, 69.9]. The agents advantage is largest where learned policies are weakest: Sols success varies by only five points across object splits (85/82/80%) and it leads on PLAN and MEM. Sol also outperforms Galaxea 0.5 on the real robot (64% vs. 53%, Sec. 5). Section 7 analyses where this advantage comes from.

sections.title: 7 LLM Agents: Harness and Model Ablations
sections.content: The LLM agents lead the leaderboard (Sec. 6). We ask what drives this: the harness that connects the language model to the robot, or the language model itself. Harnesses. All harnesses give the model the same overhead and wrist images, the same task rules and no privileged simulator state. Direct tool calls uses the inspect-robots harness [81], letting the model command end-effector motions directly through tool calls. PyRUA-Lean [30] is code-as-policy harness [45]: the model writes Python that uses open-vocabulary segmentation (via SAM3 [82]), 3D localization and inverse kinematics to move the arm. PyRUA-Lean + Galaxea 0.5 adds the fine-tuned Galaxea 0.5 policy as tool: the model localizes objects, plans, and places, while handing grasping to Galaxea 0.5; the agent inspects Galaxea 0.5s results periodically, and can initiate recoveries or take over. The simulator is paused while the model computes, so time limits apply to simulated time only. Paired episodes. Running agents on all 916 episodes is costly, so the ablations use 60 fixed primary-evaluation episodes: 30 easy episodes (six per task family) and 30 hard episodes (six per family with the fewest successes among the nine learned policies, including 11 PLAN episodes). Both sets were selected before any agent was run. The harness matters more than the model. With GPT-6.1 Sol, success rises from 35% (21/60) with direct tool calls to 67% (40/60) with PyRUA-Lean and 85% (51/60) with the Galaxea 0.5 hand-off (Fig. 9a), against 13 Figure 9: Harness and LLM ablation on the 60 paired episodes. sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: SO-101 Bench makes evaluation of language-conditioned spatial manipulation on low-cost arm both repeatable and predictive of the real robot. Its digital twin reproduces which conditions are hard and why policies fail there, and it ranks five policies trained without real data exactly as the physical SO-101 does; policies developed against the benchmark run out of the box in unseen real environments with unseen objects. The leaderboard shows where current methods stand: learned policies grasp familiar objects reliably but struggle with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning, while an LLM agent that writes code and delegates grasping to learned policy leads both in simulation and on the real robot, largely because of its harness. Limitations. The sim2real study covers five policies and 45 layouts in one real environment, so its intervals are wide (MMRV 95% CI [0.000, 0.169]), and simulation overestimates absolute success by 9 to 31 percentage points; simulated success rates should be read as an upper bound and comparisons, not levels, as what transfers. The learned policies are compared at fixed 36 fine-tuning budget, which left some of them under-trained, so the leaderboard does not measure capability ceilings. The agents time limits count simulated or control time only: the simulator pauses, and the real arm holds still, while the language model computes, which hides their real-time cost. Finally, the benchmark covers rigid objects and single arm. Extending the twin to deformable objects and bimanual setups, adding real-time constraints for agents, and using the twins ranking as prior for cheaper real-robot evaluation are natural next steps. logical next step is to use repeated rollouts in the twin to refine control programs and accumulate validated, reusable skills across episodes, as in ASPIRE [85] and RoboRSI [86], while keeping the held-out evaluation fixed.

Asset generation. We start from an image of the object: photograph of the real object, an image from the internet, or an image from text-to-image model. An image-to-3D model accessed through 3D AI Studio [71] converts it into textured mesh (GLB) with physically based rendering (PBR) materials. 2. Mesh processing (Blender). The mesh is scaled to the objects real dimensions, oriented, and given an origin at its base, which serves as the objects root pose for the success conditions. Texture colours are corrected towards the objects real palette and brightness. The mesh is then duplicated into visual and physics mesh. Visual mesh: remeshed and decimated to fixed visual budget, repaired (loose geometry removed, duplicate vertices merged, no non-manifold edges), and the original colour and roughness are baked onto it. Physics mesh: cleaned and remeshed to coarser physical budget, avoiding small crevices in which the gripper could become caught. Over-faceted results are smoothed, remaining non-manifold regions are filled or remeshed at larger voxel size, and face normals are made consistent. The physics mesh is checked to align with the visual mesh. Both meshes are exported together as USD file with packed textures. 3. Physics setup (Isaac Sim). The root prim is made rigid body with mass. The physics mesh is given collider, using signed-distance-field (SDF) collider for complex non-convex shapes without thin walls and convex hull or convex decomposition otherwise. physics material sets static and dynamic friction and restitution, and the physics mesh is hidden from rendering. 4. Appearance tuning (Isaac Lab). The visual meshs colour texture is adjusted, usually by tuning its brightness and occasionally by repainting regions, until the objects appearance under the benchmark cameras matches the real object.
